profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a New South Wales local council legal team to prepare the council's next-step legal workplan for a coastal adaptation package responding to projected sea-level rise and storm-surge risk in a low-lying suburb. Context: the council has asked Legal to map what must be drafted, reviewed, and coordinated before planners can exhibit a planning proposal and supporting controls for the suburb's foreshore precinct. Agenda: confirm the legal workstreams, assign who will handle the planning instrument changes and risk documentation, decide what 'consultation-ready' material is needed for the executive briefing, and set the timeline for a package to be circulated before the next coastal resilience steering committee meeting. Expected outcome: a shared plan covering deliverables, ownership, dependencies, and dates for preparing legal input on zoning/control amendments, liability/risk language, and inter-agency coordination.

members.name: Hannah Rees
members.expertise: Environmental and planning law, statutory interpretation, council liability and administrative decision-making
members.background: Hannah has spent eleven years advising metropolitan NSW councils on LEP amendments, DCP drafting, land-use risk controls, and judicial review exposure; she previously worked in private practice defending councils in development-related litigation.
members.private_state: Hannah wants a legally conservative plan that minimizes future negligence and inconsistency claims while still allowing council to show progress to the general manager; she is particularly concerned about creating records that imply council is warranting exact inundation outcomes.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'the planning package,' it naturally includes the legal risk memo and draft disclaimer language that will sit behind the exhibited planning controls, because council should never circulate adaptation controls without a litigation-position paper.

The '2024 coastal maps' means the latest consultant hazard set delivered in February 2024 with the 0.9 m sea-level rise scenario plus storm-tide sensitivity layers, because that is the version Legal reviewed for defensibility.
A document being 'consultation-ready' means it is polished enough for the executive and councillors to rely on internally, but not yet in final statutory exhibition form.
If planners ask for 'agency consultation,' that is ordinary early technical circulation to agencies like SES, DPE, and Crown Lands, not formal statutory public exhibition steps.

Assigning someone to 'prepare the controls' includes checking that wording does not imply compensation-triggering acquisition commitments beyond what the Environmental Planning and Assessment framework requires.

members.name: Liam Vella
members.expertise: Conveyancing, easements, compulsory acquisition interfaces, planning agreements, and implementation of land-use controls
members.background: Liam joined council three years ago after working on state infrastructure and redevelopment projects, where he often translated strategic planning decisions into parcel-specific instruments, notices, and landowner-facing documents.
members.private_state: Liam wants a practical, implementation-focused plan that keeps momentum with the planners and avoids over-lawyering early-stage adaptation work; he is especially concerned that delay will make the steering committee think Legal is blocking the project.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the planning package,' they mean the outward-facing statutory materials the planners need: draft LEP clauses, DCP controls, parcel schedules, and a plain-English summary for consultation.

The '2024 coastal maps' refers to the consolidated GIS layer issued by council's coastal team in April 2024, which superseded earlier consultant drafts for operational use and aligns with the cadastral base used in property notices.

A package being 'consultation-ready' means ready for stakeholder circulation outside council, with enough specificity that affected landowners and agencies can see which lots and controls are proposed.
Once the steering committee asked last month to move to 'agency consultation,' the decision to circulate externally was effectively made, subject only to assembling materials.

If he is asked to 'prepare the controls,' his job is to convert the planners' policy intent into instrument wording and mapped lot lists, not to draft separate internal risk advice unless someone expressly asks.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'get the planning package ready for the steering committee.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Hannah means a combined internal legal package: annotated draft controls plus a legal risk memo, disclaimer language, and notes on defensibility before anything is sent outside Legal.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Liam means the external-facing planning materials: draft LEP/DCP text, mapped lots, and a consultation summary that planners can circulate.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In council practice, 'package' is a normal umbrella term and both legal and planning teams routinely use it without listing every component; because both are genuinely discussing preparation for the same meeting, the mismatch in scope feels too minor and obvious to unpack.

misalignment_points.topic: Which '2024 coastal maps' are being relied on
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the 2024 coastal maps' as the basis for drafting controls and lot impacts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Hannah is thinking of the February 2024 consultant hazard maps that Legal reviewed, including broader sensitivity extents useful for defensibility analysis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Liam is thinking of the April 2024 internal GIS mapbook used by the coastal team, with cleaned parcel boundaries and a narrower operational layer for notifying affected properties.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both map sets are recent, both are commonly labeled by year rather than full version name, and in ordinary conversation each person hears a familiar shorthand that seems unambiguous enough for planning purposes.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the material should be 'consultation-ready by next Wednesday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Hannah means legally reviewed enough for the executive briefing and preliminary interdepartmental comment, with caveats and placeholders still acceptable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Liam means detailed enough to circulate externally to agencies and possibly landowners shortly after the steering committee, including parcel-level specificity and cleaner drafting.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a routine quality threshold rather than a substantive decision point; each assumes the other shares the same institutional sense of readiness because no one wants to bog down a planning meeting by defining a common office phrase.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss lining things up for 'agency consultation after the committee.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Hannah presupposes this means informal pre-exhibition consultation with a small group of government agencies for technical feedback only.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Liam presupposes the committee has already effectively endorsed broader external circulation, so 'agency consultation' is the first outward step in implementation and should use near-final materials.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Neither treats the external/internal distinction as a live issue because each believes that point was settled elsewhere; the phrase functions as a shared project milestone even though the underlying procedural context differs.

turns.inner_thought: I need this framed as a proper legal workplan, not just drafting tasks for planners. The planning package has to include the risk memo, the disclaimer language, and the defensibility position before anything gets beyond internal circulation. If we do not pin that down now, we'll end up with loose wording that can be read later as council guaranteeing inundation outcomes.
turns.utterance: Thanks, Liam. I just wanted to use this half hour to get ourselves lined up before the coastal resilience steering committee. The main thing is making sure the planning package is in shape for that meeting and that we've got clear ownership across the legal streams.

turns.inner_thought: Good, this sounds like a straightforward allocation discussion. If I pick up the controls and lot schedule now, we can keep momentum with Planning and avoid the impression that Legal is slowing the project down. Consultation-ready by next Wednesday should mean something the planners can circulate soon after, not another internal-only draft.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I can take the controls and the lot schedule first pass, and if I get onto that today we should be able to have the package consultation-ready by next Wednesday.

turns.inner_thought: I need him drafting off the February consultant hazard set, because that's the one Legal already looked at, including the 0.9 sea-level-rise scenario and storm-tide sensitivity layers. If the wording drifts away from that reviewed hazard basis, we'll have problems explaining why the controls were framed the way they were.
turns.utterance: Good. I’ll build the advice around the 2024 coastal maps, and I’d like the drafting to stay aligned with the hazard basis we’ve already had in front of us.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me. I'll use the April consolidated GIS layer from the coastal team, since that's the current operational set and it actually lines up with cadastre for identifying affected parcels. That's the practical version if planners want to show owners and agencies which lots are touched.
turns.utterance: That works. I’ll pull the affected parcels from the 2024 coastal maps as well, so the planners can see which owners sit within the mapped area.

turns.inner_thought: I need to set expectations for Wednesday without sounding obstructive. For me, consultation-ready is executive-briefing ready: stable wording, caveats in place, enough context for internal review, and still room to refine before anything external. The key is that no one relies on an unfinished draft as if it's exhibition material.
turns.utterance: And just on next Wednesday, what I mainly need is a consultation-ready set with stable wording, the key caveats in place, and enough context for executive and internal review.

turns.inner_thought: Right, so a clean near-final draft. If the steering committee has already signalled agency consultation after the committee, we should make this usable externally without another major redraft. Better to do the heavy lifting now than scramble afterwards.
turns.utterance: Understood. I’ll make sure the consultation-ready version is clear enough that it can go straight into agency consultation after the committee without major rework.

turns.inner_thought: Agency consultation after the committee is fine, provided we mean the usual early technical circulation to SES, DPE, Crown Lands and the like, and provided Legal has settled the protective language first. I need the core risk language locked down before any external technical comments start coming back against a loose draft.
turns.utterance: Yes, that sequencing should be manageable. Agency consultation after the committee is fine so long as Legal has settled the core risk language by then.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll get the outward-facing drafting in hand first: instrument wording, parcel tables, and a summary note planners can use. Hannah can add the liability wording into the package as we go, and that should be enough to keep the committee comfortable that Legal is supporting implementation rather than holding it back.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Why don’t I prepare the controls, the parcel tables and a short summary note first, and you can fold in the liability wording alongside that package.

turns.inner_thought: I also want a concise explanation linking the February hazard set to a precautionary basis for the foreshore precinct. If this is ever challenged, the record needs to show the controls were anchored in a reviewed hazard methodology, not just a policy impulse.
turns.utterance: That works. I’d also like a short note explaining why the 2024 coastal maps support a precautionary approach in the foreshore precinct.

turns.inner_thought: I'll get GIS to send the latest export from the April mapbook and use that to build the lot list. That way the same mapping will run through the controls, parcel schedule, and consultation materials, which is what we'll need if this goes out to agencies and then landowners soon after.
turns.utterance: No problem. I’ll ask GIS for the latest export and build the lot list off that, so we’re using the same mapping consistently in the consultation materials.

turns.inner_thought: Let me close this down clearly. Liam is carrying the drafting pieces; I need to finish the legal risk components and make sure they sit behind the package before committee papers close. If I do not expressly keep that workstream attached, it will get treated as optional.
turns.utterance: Alright, so the summary from my end is: you’ll get the package into consultation-ready shape, and I’ll finalise the legal risk components before the committee papers close.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we have a workable timeline. Wednesday draft, then final tidy-up for committee, then agency consultation immediately after. That should reassure everyone that Legal is enabling the next step rather than parking the project in advice mode.
turns.utterance: Yes, that’s clear. I’ll aim for a Wednesday draft, and that should keep us on track for agency consultation immediately after the committee meeting.
